newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-India's "Big Bull" sees boom times ahead.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-India's "Big Bull" sees boom times ahead.

text.p: Controversial stockbroker Harshad Mehta said on Wednesday he expects Indian shares to boom because of a stronger rupee and higher capital inflows which will push interest rates down, tame inflation and boost companies' bottom line.

Two developments in recent months -- opening Indian markets to foreign debt funds and allowing Indian firms to raise loans up to $100 million abroad without restriction -- would make cash cheaper, he told Reuters in an interview.
Several blue-chip Indian firms are planning to raise funds abroad at between 6.5 percent and 9.0 percent in dollar terms compared to domestic interest rates of 14 percent to 16 percent, he said.
"Uptil now we have been seeing the dollar rising and rupee devaluing," he said. "Today we have equal chance of rupee upvaluation."

India's foreign exchange reserves currently total $27.29 billion against $21.86 billion a year ago. The Reserve Bank of India figures show the central bank bought $2.3 billion in March to keep the rupee from appreciating.
"The rupee will appreciate," he said. "It is only the government that is stopping it."
Mehta was nicknamed "Big Bull" for his controversial role in the early 1990s stocks boom. The bubble burst when he was accused of illegally diverting funds from government securities into shares.
Arrested and held in jail until he got bail Mehta faces several court cases but he has not been convicted of any wrongdoing.
Mehta said it was a wrong notion that exports would be hit when the currency became stronger.
"Price is related to perceptions, not on performance," he said.

A stronger rupee would make dollar debts cheaper for both companies and the government, he said. Cheaper imports would keep inflation under control while higher capital inflows would bring down interest rates.
"Exports will slow temporarily but will pick up as their costs come down," he said.
In the last quarter of 1996 the Supreme Court allowed Mehta and others accused in the 1992 scam to resume work. He has since been sought by foreign and domestic funds for investment advise.
Financial restructuring is the most crucial factor to watch in a company when you look at investing in a stock, he said.

Now he plans to target retail investors by identifying stocks which offer good bargains. He noted that investors put money in unsecured deposits at 14.5-15 percent interest in a company but would not buy the same firm's stock which gave dividend yield of 17 percent, he said.
"I have always observed that classes make money, masses make the market," he said. "I want to be an ambassador of investors."
He plans to do this by putting his stocks recommendation on the internet beginning early in June.
